title: Chapter 2 — That The Notions Of Democratic Nations On Government Are Naturally Favorable To The Concentration Of Power
paragraphs: Naturally Favorable To The Concentration Of Power

The notion of secondary powers, placed between the sovereign and his subjects, came naturally to the imagination of aristocratic nations, because those communities contained individuals or families raised above the common level and apparently destined to command by birth, education, and wealth. This same notion is naturally missing from the minds of men in democratic ages, for the opposite reasons. It can only be introduced artificially, and it can only be kept there with difficulty. They conceive, almost without thinking about it, the notion of a single central power that governs the whole community by its direct influence. Moreover, in politics as in philosophy and religion, the intellect of democratic nations is particularly open to simple and general ideas. Complicated systems are distasteful to it, and its favorite conception is that of a great nation composed of citizens all resembling the same pattern, and all governed by a single power.

The very next notion to that of a single central power, which presents itself to the minds of men in ages of equality, is the notion of uniformity of legislation. Since every man sees that he differs very little from those around him, he cannot understand why a rule that applies to one should not apply equally to all the rest. Even the slightest privileges are therefore offensive to his reason, the faintest differences in the political institutions of the same people shock him, and uniformity of legislation seems to him the first condition of good government. I find, by contrast, that this same notion of a uniform rule binding equally on all members of the community was almost unknown to the human mind in aristocratic ages — either never entertained, or rejected. These opposing tendencies of opinion ultimately settle on each side into such blind instincts and ungovernable habits that they still direct men's actions, despite particular exceptions. Despite the immense variety of conditions in the Middle Ages, a certain number of persons lived then in exactly similar circumstances; yet this did not prevent the laws of the time from assigning each of them distinct duties and different rights. Today, on the contrary, all the powers of government are exerted to impose the same customs and the same laws on populations that as yet have few points of resemblance. As the conditions of men become equal within a people, individuals seem less important and society seems larger — or rather, every citizen, assimilated to all the rest, is lost in the crowd, and nothing stands out but the great and imposing image of the people as a whole. This naturally gives the men of democratic periods a lofty opinion of the privileges of society and a very humble notion of the rights of individuals. They are ready to admit that the interests of the former are everything and the interests of the latter nothing. They are willing to grant that the power representing the community has far more information and wisdom than any of its members, and that it is the duty as well as the right of that power to guide as well as govern each private citizen.

If we examine our contemporaries closely and press down to the root of their political opinions, we will find some of the notions I have just described. We may even be surprised to find such agreement between men who are so often at odds. The Americans hold that in every state the supreme power should come from the people. But once that power is constituted, they can conceive almost no limits to it, and they are ready to admit that it has the right to do whatever it pleases. They have not the slightest notion of special privileges granted to cities, families, or persons. It seems never to have occurred to them that one might not apply the same laws with strict uniformity to every part and to every inhabitant. These same opinions are spreading more and more in Europe. They are insinuating themselves even among those nations that most vehemently reject the principle of popular sovereignty. Such nations attribute a different origin to supreme power, but they ascribe to that power the same characteristics. Among them all, the idea of intermediate powers is weakening and being erased. The idea of rights inherent in certain individuals is rapidly disappearing from men's minds, and the idea of the omnipotence and sole authority of society as a whole rises to fill its place. These ideas take root and spread as social conditions become more equal and men more alike. They are produced by equality, and they in turn hasten equality's progress.

In France, where the revolution I am speaking of has gone further than in any other European country, these opinions have completely taken hold of the public mind. If we listen carefully to the language of the various parties in France, we find that there is not one that has not adopted them. Most of these parties criticize the conduct of the government, but they all hold that the government ought perpetually to act and interfere in everything that is done. Even those parties most at odds with one another agree on this point. The unity, ubiquity, and omnipotence of the supreme power, together with the uniformity of its rules, form the chief characteristics of every political system put forward in our age. They recur even in the wildest visions of political regeneration. The human mind pursues them even in its dreams. If these notions arise spontaneously in the minds of private individuals, they suggest themselves still more forcefully to the minds of princes. As the ancient fabric of European society is altered and dissolved, sovereigns acquire new conceptions of their opportunities and duties. They learn for the first time that the central power they represent may and should administer, through its own agents and on a uniform plan, all the affairs of the whole community. This opinion — which, I venture to say, had never been conceived by the monarchs of Europe before our time — now sinks deeply into the minds of kings and remains there amid all the stirring of less settled thoughts.

Our contemporaries are therefore much less divided than is commonly supposed. They constantly argue over whose hands supremacy should be placed in, but they readily agree on the duties and rights of that supremacy. The notion they all form of government is that of a single, simple, providential, and creative power. All secondary opinions in politics are unsettled; this one remains fixed, invariable, and consistent. It is adopted by statesmen and political philosophers; it is eagerly seized by the multitude. Those who govern and those who are governed agree to pursue it with equal ardor. It is the foremost notion in their minds; it seems inborn. It originates, then, in no whim of the human intellect, but is a necessary condition of the present state of mankind.
